item.title: Structural evolution of an ancient nucleotidyltransferase underlies divergence of AbiE antitoxins.
item.author: Liu T, Chen R, Tang K, Yao J, Chen Z, Liu Z, Guo Y, Genevaux P, Xu X, Wang X.
item.description:
Type VII toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems neutralize toxins through antitoxin-mediated post-translational modification (PTM), with the oligoAMPylation-based HepT/MntA and phosphorylation-based AbiE systems representing the most prevalent families. Although the AbiE TA system from Mycobacterium tuberculosis is known to employ antitoxin-dependent phosphorylation to antagonize its toxin, the overall distribution and regulatory diversity of AbiE-like systems remain obscure. A comprehensive search of the IMG/M database revealed that AbiE TA systems comprise a conserved toxin family paired with six distinct groups of antitoxins, including four newly identified antitoxin groups. Despite extensive sequence divergence, structural predictions indicate that most of these antitoxins share a conserved winged helix-turn-helix (wHTH) domain and a C-terminal structurally homologous domain (CTD). item.title: Welwitschia leaf senescence is orchestrated via ERF113-ERF115-mediated antagonism between hormone signaling pathways.
item.author: Xu H, Song Q, Mamo W, Tolosa LN, Zhang J, Aboushanab AGMF, Wang Q, Wan T.
item.description:
Phytohormone crosstalk is fundamental to plant development and adaptation. While the coordinated actions of different hormones are well recognized, the underlying molecular mechanisms in specific biological processes remain largely elusive. Here, we identified the WmERF113-WmERF115 module as a central hub that mediated jasmonic acid (JA)/abscisic acid (ABA)-gibberellins (GA) antagonism to regulate leaf senescence in Welwitschia, a desert plant with only two leaves that grow continuously over an exceptionally long lifespan. We revealed that the JA/ABA-inducible transcription factor (TF) WmERF113 directly activated senescence-associated genes (SAGs), promoting senescence and chlorophyll degradation, whereas the GA-responsive WmERF115 repressed the same targets to mitigate senescence. item.title: Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K-12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act.
item.author: Rodríguez Ferrante G, Dasika NS, Nam A, Lu J, Tumber N, Kully-Rivera E, Klei V, Zhang D, Romero ME, de la Iglesia HO.
item.description:
The US House's approval of the Sunshine Protection Act has revived the debate between permanent daylight saving time (DST) and standard time (ST). Permanent DST would push school start times before sunrise in many regions. Health, sleep, and scientific organizations favor permanent ST because it keeps solar, biological, and social time better aligned, 1 which matters most for children and adolescents, whose rigid school schedules already conflict with their biological night and are linked to poor sleep and reduced cognitive and academic performance. 2 , 3 , 4 The safety consequences of the proposed change remain unquantified, but for children, morning light availability matters most, since most return home in daylight regardless of clock policy. item.title: The rise and diversification of spidroins in the deep-time evolution of spiders.
item.author: Jiang T, Jin P, Zhang Y, Wu M, Shen Y, Zhao Z, Xin Y, Pisani D, Donoghue PCJ, Li S.
item.description:
The evolutionary success of spiders is often attributed to their stunning ability to produce and utilize silk, but the potential link between the molecular and phenotypic basis of silk production and spider diversification is seldom tested in a robust dated phylogenetic framework. Here, we provide a macroevolutionary context for testing hypotheses by reconstructing and dating the spider tree of life using genomic and transcriptomic data. We searched exhaustively for members of the spider silk protein (spidroin) gene family from omics data and identified them in an iterative phylogenetic pipeline. Four distinct new types of spidroins with atypical sequence characteristics are discovered to be widespread in true spiders with the potential to affect silk properties, as inferred by our phylogenetic generalized linear mixed model and phylogenetic generalized least squares analyses. item.title: Primary cilia mediate specific neuron-glia attachments in C. elegans through the secreted protein BUG-1.
item.author: Wexler LR, Griffin B, Dutta P, Sengupta P, Kolotuev I, Ringstad N, Heiman MG.
item.description:
Primary cilia are signaling hubs that influence nearly every aspect of cell physiology. Neuronal primary cilia were recently found to form extensive attachments to glia in the mammalian brain, but it is not known how these attachments form or what functions they serve. Defects in cilia cause profound neurological disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the specialized functions of neuronal cilia. Here, we use a genetic screen in Caenorhabditis elegans to determine how a stereotyped cilia-glia attachment forms and how the attachment affects ciliary calcium signaling. We find that two sensory neurons (URX and BAG) use their cilia to attach to a specific glial partner (ILsoL/R). This attachment requires BUG-1, a large secreted protein that localizes precisely to the cilia-glia attachment site. item.title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation.
item.author: Lv P, Chen D, Zhang C, Zhang K, Wang L.
item.description:
Knowing which way you are facing is essential for navigation. In animals, a dedicated set of neurons-head direction cells-acts as an internal compass: each cell fires most strongly when the animal faces a particular direction. The anterior thalamus is a key hub for this system. In humans, however, direct electrophysiological evidence for a comparable head direction signal remains limited. To address this gap, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) from the anteroventral thalamus (AVT) in patients with epilepsy while they performed a virtual navigation task. We analyzed neural activity during in-place rotation to isolate virtual head direction (vHD) information. item.title: Effector-triggered immunity in oilseed crops is expanded despite the restricted specificity of the receptor ZAR1.
item.author: Breit-McNally C, Lai Y, Xiao R, Mazzurco O, Lyons C, Singh RA, Martel A, Seto D, Parkin IAP, Desveaux D, Guttman DS.
item.description:
Effector-triggered immunity (ETI), mediated by nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat immune receptors (NLRs), plays a critical role in protecting plants from pathogens. While the scope of ETI elicited by Pseudomonas syringae type III effectors on Arabidopsis thaliana has been characterized, no equivalent study has been performed on related oilseed crops, limiting our ability to translate fundamental plant immunity research into crop protection strategies. Here, we present a comprehensive screen of the ETI landscapes in Brassicaceous oilseeds Brassica napus (canola) and Camelina sativa (false flax) using 529 P. syringae effectors. We found that 44.6% and 55.4% of the 65 effector families contained alleles that elicited ETI in B. napus and C. sativa, respectively. item.title: Avian germline-restricted chromosomes are reservoirs for active and expressed long-terminal-repeat retroviruses.
item.author: Fang B, Edwards SV.
item.description:
Germline-restricted chromosomes (GRCs) occur only in germ cells and are absent from somatic cells in songbirds, but their contents and evolutionary mechanisms remain poorly understood. We performed comparative genomics on long-read GRC assemblies from male house finch (HF) (Haemorhous mexicanus), common rosefinch (RF) (Carpodacus erythrinus), and blue tit (Cyanistes caeruleus), the first two of which are newly assembled and annotated. The assemblies vary widely in size (6.5-168.4 Mb) and gene content; whereas most GRC-linked genes are species specific, a small conserved set predates the diversification of passerine birds 47 mya. Despite genic variability, GRCs are consistently repeat rich (63.7%-79.5%) and accumulate intact endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) with long terminal repeats (LTRs). item.title: Infants respond to alterations in their own voice months before they recognize themselves in the mirror.
item.author: Belia M, Fabre F, Borel C, Aucouturier JJ, Faivre N, Goupil L.
item.description:
Recognizing our body as our own grounds our perceptions, actions, and social interactions. Even newborns detect cross-modal links between self-related perceptions, 1 considered necessary for body ownership. 2 Yet, clear evidence for a sense of ownership only appears once children not simply detect but also correct mismatches between predicted and perceived self-related sensorimotor inputs.
